transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SE), Rajiv Patel (Borealis Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (Platform), Tom Liu (Eng Manager), Aisha Khan (Security)

Auto-summary: short intake focusing on unit economics. Customer is cost sensitive, wants concrete per-token examples and a path to dedicated/private later.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for joining — can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Rajiv Patel: Yep, loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:05] Maya Chen: Cool. Quick intros. I'll hand it to Rajiv to give a 60-second on what you're trying to build and the constraints.
[00:12] Rajiv Patel: Sure. So Borealis is building a customer-facing summarization and routing layer for enterprise support tickets. We're doing multimodal ingestion but 80% is text, average prompt ~220 tokens, responses ~350 tokens. Primary constraint: cost per interaction and predictability for monthly budgeting. We have a p95 latency target of ~250 milliseconds for the main route, and some background jobs can be slower.
[00:42] Ethan Park: Got it. When you say p95 250ms, is that for the whole end-to-end or just model token latency?
[00:48] Sofia Martinez: For the main route it's end-to-end. We break out external calls, but the app needs the model piece to be sub 200 ideally.
[00:55] Lina Gomez: That's helpful. A couple clarifying q's: are you currently hosting anything on-prem or fully cloud?
[01:02] Tom Liu: We're all cloud today — GCP predominately, some GKE, we use Vault for KMS and Okta for SSO.
[01:08] Aisha Khan: Security is important for us. SOC2 Type II and key management integration, audit logs — those are checkboxes.
[01:15] Maya Chen: Great. High level we support three deployment paths — hosted API for fastest onboarding, dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput and costs, and private (VPC/on-prem) for regulated needs. Today we'll focus on unit economics and a pilot plan.
[01:26] Rajiv Patel: Perfect. We ran some quick numbers internally. With our current traffic model, any per-token price above $0.0006 puts us over budget; below $0.00035 looks ideal. But we know advertised pricing can vary depending on batching, context length, and embeddings. Curious how Redwood thinks about that.
[01:42] Ethan Park: Yeah, that's a great starting point. A few levers we typically point at: batching (how many concurrent requests you can combine), KV/prefix caching (re-using cached key/value states across similar prompts), sequence length quantization/quantization friendly engines, and routing to cheaper model variants for non-critical paths. Also reserved dedicated pools change the effective per-token cost versus hosted burst pricing.
[02:02] Rajiv Patel: Can you unpack batching and how it affects latency?
[02:06] Ethan Park: Sure — so batching increases throughput by grouping in-flight requests into a single GPU pass; effective cost per token drops, but you add batching delay. Redwood's runtime uses dynamic batching with max latency caps — so we won't wait longer than a configured window. Practically you tune batch window so that for your 250ms p95 route we have micro-batching of like 8–16 ms windows, with small gains. For heavy traffic, batching yields big savings. For lowQPS but bursty traffic, prefix/KV caching often gives the best bang for buck.
[02:40] Sofia Martinez: When you say prefix caching, are you referring to keeping the KV cache warm per session? We have a lot of similar prompts per customer.
[02:46] Lina Gomez: Exactly. If you have recurring prefixes — e.g., standard instruction prompts — we can cache the KV states so subsequent calls only decode the new tokens. That reduces compute roughly proportional to the saved prefix length. The caching hit rate is what matters.
[02:58] Tom Liu: What about embeddings? We're doing reranking; that's a separate cost center.
[03:02] Ethan Park: Embeddings are charged differently — typically per embedding vector. For reranking we often suggest batching embeddings requests separately and storing vectors to avoid re-embedding unchanged content. For unit econ, we'll show an example sheet.
[03:14] Rajiv Patel: On dedicated — if we commit to reserved capacity, how deterministic is the price per token?
[03:19] Maya Chen: With Dedicated you get a committed monthly capacity and a significantly lower effective per-token price because the infra cost is amortized. We provide example amortization scenarios: e.g., for a T4-equivalent pool vs an A100-like pool the numbers change. We'll include sample amortization in the pricing sheet.
[03:34] Rajiv Patel: Do you support hybrid — hosted for low-priority/edge and dedicated for high-priority routes?
[03:38] Ethan Park: Yes — smart routing can pin critical routes to dedicated and fall back to hosted or cheaper model variants if dedicated is saturated. This is a common pattern we recommend for budget-constrained teams.
[03:48] Aisha Khan: About security — can you integrate with our Vault KMS, and do you provide customer-managed keys for private?
[03:54] Lina Gomez: For Private deployments we support integrating your KMS — yes. For Hosted we provide envelope encryption and options for bringing keys via KMS connectors; there are additional compliance reviews for customer-managed KMS in hosted mode, which we'll detail. Audit logs and SSO/SAML are supported across Enterprise plans.
[04:12] Rajiv Patel: Cool. For the pilot, our idea was: 2–4 week hosted pilot using a production-like traffic replay, then a 2-week dedicated spike to compare unit economics. Does that make sense from Redwood's side?
[04:23] Maya Chen: That makes total sense. Typical pilot flow we recommend: 1) hosted smoke + integration test, 2) run a 48–72 hour throughput benchmark with replayed traffic and our perf hooks, 3) if numbers justify, spin up a dedicated pilot with reserved capacity for 2 weeks to measure amortized cost.
[04:40] Tom Liu: For the benchmark, what instrumentation do you need?
[04:44] Ethan Park: We'll provide a runbook and a small client script that emits requests at various QPS and records token-level timing — request arrival, queue delay, batch size, model latency, decode time. Also hooks for tracing so you can map back to your APM. We'll share the script after the call.
[04:59] Rajiv Patel: Pricing specifics: give me an example. Say we have 200k requests/day, avg tokens in/out ~570 total. What's a rough hosted vs dedicated cost ballpark?
[05:08] Maya Chen: We'll compute precise numbers in the sheet, but ballpark: hosted might be X per 1M tokens at baseline; with batching and caching you could see 10–40% reductions; dedicated if utilization is high enough can cut another 30–60% depending on model/hardware. (note: numbers intentionally left high level here).
[05:29] Sofia Martinez: The team cares about predictability — how do you handle overages on dedicated?
[05:33] Maya Chen: Dedicated contracts include burst policies — small bursts covered within pool; if sustained overage occurs, routing policies kick in (fallback to hosted or degraded model variant). We can set alerts and throttles to avoid surprise bills.
[05:44] Rajiv Patel: Any latency penalties with quantized models? Our app is latency-sensitive.
[05:48] Ethan Park: Typically quantized models run faster and cheaper on modern runtimes, though some micro-ops can introduce small variance. In our experience post-quantization we still meet strict p95 targets for short sequences, but we'll validate with the benchmark.
[05:59] Tom Liu: Are there limitations on model size with caching?
[06:02] Lina Gomez: Not really; caching is largely orthogonal — it relates to KV state length. Larger models may have larger KV states but the caching benefit scales. We also support trimmed contexts and chunking strategies.
[06:12] Rajiv Patel: One more question on measurements: how do you define tokens? We saw different tokenizers across models and vendors.
[06:17] Ethan Park: Great point. Redwood reports token counts per the model's tokenizer and normalizes billing to the model variant used. In the pricing sheet we'll show per-model tokenization examples so you can map your prompts.
[06:27] Aisha Khan: From a compliance perspective, if we go hosted, what are the controls for data residency and log retention?
[06:33] Maya Chen: Hosted supports region selection; for strict residency and retention policies we recommend Dedicated or Private. Hosted can restrict retention windows and provide audit logs, but some customers with strict residency choose Private so data never leaves their VPC.
[06:46] Rajiv Patel: Awesome. Any friction points others typically hit?
[06:49] Ethan Park: Two common ones — unexpected tokenization assumptions (they impact unit cost), and hit rates on caching being lower than expected. We usually recommend a brief analysis of prompt variance beforehand. Also planning for tail-latency when you mix long sequences into a short-p99 environment.
[07:06] Sofia Martinez: Okay so next practicals — we'll want the pricing sheet, the benchmark runbook, and an SLO template.
[07:12] Maya Chen: We'll send those. Also, we'll include a worked example with your approximate numbers (200k/day, 570 tokens) so you can see hosted vs dedicated amortized.
[07:20] Rajiv Patel: Timeline — we want procurement/approval by mid-April. If we run the hosted pilot in late March that fits.
[07:26] Maya Chen: Sounds good. We'll target sending materials by Friday.
[07:29] Tom Liu: One last quick thing — competitors. We're also talking to Hugging Face for self-host and OpenAI for hosted comparisons.
[07:36] Maya Chen: Totally expected. We'll include comparative notes (where applicable) and model parity checks.
[07:40] Rajiv Patel: Thanks, everyone.
[07:42] Maya Chen: Thanks — recap and next steps.

Recap (quick):
- Redwood to send pricing sheet with sample per-token math, dedicated amortization table, and recommended routing pattern.
- Redwood SE to send benchmarking runbook & client script.
- Borealis to provide traffic profile and p95 target confirmation.
- Tentative pilot: hosted late-March, dedicated spike after hosted results; procurement target mid-April.
